newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top U.N. envoy in Burundi welcomes changes.
newsitem.headline: Top U.N. envoy in Burundi welcomes changes.

text.p: The top U.N. representative to Burundi on Friday welcomed a decision by Burundi's military leaders to restore parliament and lift the ban on political parties, saying they were steps "in the right direction".
Marc Faguy, special representative of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, also revealed that the number of U.N. human rights observers in Burundi would be doubled to 10.
The military government of Major Pierre Buyoya announced on Thursday it was immediately lifting bans on all political parties and the national assembly imposed since a July 25 coup.
"This is a move in the right direction. It is an excellent initiative of Major Buyoya," Faguy, a former Canadian diplomat, told a news briefing.
"I assume from the declaration this is the same National Assembly as was elected in 1993," he added.

In Bujumbura, Burundi's rebels and main Tutsi and Hutu parties dismissed the lifting as a bid to loosen the grip of economic sanctions imposed by regional states. The embargo is aimed at forcing the government to hold talks with all political parties, including Hutu rebels.

The increase in observers, which Faguy discussed with U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Jose Ayala-Lasso in Geneva on Friday, followed a written government request for the number to be "considerably increased", according to U.N. officials.

"Mr. Buyoya and his new government have specifically asked for an increase in the programme of observers of human rights in Burundi," Faguy said. "There is a decision already made to increase the number of observers by at least double.
"I believe this is also a favourable development...I do believe they have a deterrent effect on violence but it is very difficult to evaluate precisely," he added.
The new human rights observers are to be appointed by the Geneva-based U.N. Centre for Human Rights run by Ayala-Lasso.
